1125.bp: When a search or question system pulls facts from the internet to answer you, those facts come from real websites and documents written by real people with real beliefs. If a chunk of the web leans left or right politically, the system will absorb that tilt and repeat it back to you, making it seem like objective truth when it's actually one perspective.
1125.wh: The difficulty is that bias isn't one mistake but a chain of them: first, the underlying documents are biased; second, a search mechanism picks biased documents; third, the language model then writes answers informed by those slanted sources. Each stage amplifies the problem, and fixing one stage doesn't stop the others. You can't just tell the model 'be fair' because the problem lives in the data it's asked to reason about.
1125.ap: They built a system with three coordinated parts. First, they tagged thousands of web documents with labels of political stance using multiple language models so bias isn't missed. Second, they stored those tags in a database so a retrieval system can see them. Third, they added a 'fairness engine' at three points in the pipeline—when searching, when ranking, and when generating—so that each step actively counters the bias rather than just avoiding it.
1125.ww: The intuition is that bias is structural and cumulative, so you have to fight it structurally at every gate. By making political stance visible (through labels), searchable (through metadata), and actionable (through fairness rules at each stage), you give the system a way to course-correct instead of blindly following biased data. It's like installing filters at the water inlet, the pump, and the tap.
1125.po: On a large test set of real questions and web documents, the system improved balance of political perspectives by 5.6% on average and lifted a fairness score dramatically—from 53.2 to 97.5—while keeping answer quality high (the facts stayed true, the answers stayed faithful to sources). The key win is that all three pieces had to work together; each alone was insufficient.

1126.bp: Visual question answering means asking 'what's in this image?' in plain English and getting a useful answer. Adding outside knowledge—facts from a database—makes this possible for questions that go beyond what the image alone shows (e.g., 'what breed is this dog?'). But the knowledge has to be structured and linked so the system finds the right facts, not a jumble of irrelevant ones.
1126.wh: Existing systems dump unstructured text into a retrieval pool and pick the top hits by keyword similarity, which works for simple factual lookup but fails when you need to know how entities (like dog breeds and characteristics) relate to each other. A jumbled list of facts confuses the language model. The system also doesn't link visual information (what it sees in the image) to semantic information (what the database knows) clearly, so it can't bridge the gap between 'I see a brown dog' and 'this is a Labrador'.
1126.ap: They build a multi-step machine-readable knowledge graph that stores entities (dog, Labrador, brown) and relationships (has-color, is-breed-of) with both text and image information attached. A language model first extracts entities and relations from documents. Then a retrieval mechanism uses both the image content and the question to navigate the graph intelligently, pulling out subgraphs (small chunks of related facts) rather than unordered lists. This keeps the structure intact.
1126.ww: Knowledge graphs work because they preserve meaning through structure. Instead of searching 1000 sentences for relevant facts, the system can say 'start at dog, follow the is-breed relation, and reach Labrador.' When visual and text information are both anchored to the same entities, the image and the knowledge pull in the same direction, so the final language model sees a coherent story instead of static snippets.
1126.po: The system can now answer more difficult visual questions correctly by retrieving smaller, more focused sets of facts that actually relate to what's visible and being asked, rather than top-n candidates by similarity. The structured retrieval also makes the answer traceable: you can see which entities and links the system used to answer you.

1127.bp: When a system retrieves facts to answer questions, the real unit that matters is not the whole document or even the paragraph—it's the atomic fact or claim (a 'nugget' of information). If facts become outdated or contradicted, the system needs to know which facts are still valid right now, not just retrieve documents and hope.
1127.wh: Standard retrieval treats a passage like a static block. But the world changes: a person's birthplace doesn't change, but their job does, and their job from three years ago may be wrong now. If multiple sources say different things, an old system just ranks them by relevance and picks the top one, potentially surfacing contradictions. There's no way to flag outdated or conflicting information to the language model.
1127.ap: Instead of storing passages, they store individual fact-nuggets with metadata: links to the sources that proved it, a date range when it was true, and a status flag (current, outdated, disputed). Before ranking nuggets for retrieval, the system filters out any nugget marked as outdated or outside its validity window. This means outdated information is removed before it reaches the language model, and conflicting claims can be flagged to the user.
1127.ww: Treating facts as versioned, tracked records mirrors how humans reason: we know facts have sources, validity periods, and sometimes disagreements. By making these properties explicit in the data structure, the system can enforce correctness automatically rather than asking the language model to guess. It's like labeling every piece of information with 'as of when' and 'still valid?' before using it.
1127.po: On question-answering tasks, the system recalled correct facts 42% more often, reduced factual errors in answers by 9 percentage points, and halved the rate of contradictions (from 2% to 1%). As a bonus, facts stored as nuggets take less space, so the system can run even in a web browser or on a phone with limited memory, not just on powerful servers.

1128.bp: Searching for a person using text ('find me a woman in a red coat') is hard because you have two modalities—language and images—that don't naturally align. Real systems use synthetic training data (fake images and descriptions) to learn the connection, then deploy on real searches where the distribution is different, and their learned patterns break.
1128.wh: Training on synthetic data and testing on real data is a fundamental mismatch. Synthetic data is clean, balanced, and grammatically perfect; real captions are messy, colloquial, and biased. The model learns spurious patterns from the synthetic world that don't transfer. Existing solutions either require massive amounts of labeled real data (impractical due to privacy rules) or rely on confidence scores that are often overconfident—the model is certain when it shouldn't be.
1128.ap: They propose a test-time adaptation method that works at deployment without needing labeled real data. The system makes two parallel searches—image-to-text and text-to-image—and measures when they 'agree' (both rank the same person highly). If they disagree, the system is uncertain, and it recalibrates its internal confidence scores and learns new patterns in real time on the real data it's actually seeing. No human annotation needed.
1128.ww: The reason this works is that disagreement is a natural signal of uncertainty. If an image looks like many people and a text description fits many people, but they don't match each other, that's a warning flag. By explicitly detecting this warning flag and using it to adjust the model's behavior, the system avoids false confidence and adapts to the real-world distribution as it encounters new examples.
1128.po: The system now works reliably in deployment without needing large labeled real-world datasets (which are hard to collect due to privacy). It reduces false positives by detecting uncertainty, and it improves accuracy as it encounters more real data over time. This makes cross-modal person search practical for real systems where privacy and scarcity of annotations are hard constraints.

1129.bp: In social networks, recommendation systems, or collaboration graphs, finding tight-knit groups is useful—maybe you want friend groups for social recommendations or product bundles that often buy together. A tight-knit group is one where people or items connect to each other densely, not just two or three friends but a cohesive cluster.
1129.wh: Real graphs are sparse: not everyone connects to everyone else, so most candidate groups are thin and loose. Existing algorithms use greedy heuristics that are fast but don't guarantee they find the largest or densest group, and they can get stuck in weak local clusters. More importantly, enforcing a density constraint—'this group must have at least X% of possible connections'—is hard without checking every subgraph, which is computationally expensive.
1129.ap: They introduce a lightweight process that ranks vertices (people or items) by an energy-diffusion principle: a vertex is more valuable if it's well-connected to other valuable vertices (recursive notion). This ranking identifies promising starting points for search. From these points, the algorithm builds candidate groups and refines them by removing low-degree vertices until the density constraint is satisfied. The result is guaranteed to meet the density requirement.
1129.ww: Energy diffusion naturally finds well-connected cores: a vertex with many connections to poorly-connected neighbors still diffuses less energy than one surrounded by well-connected neighbors. This prioritization guides the search toward dense regions of the graph instead of sparse ones. By building from a good seed and refining outward, the algorithm avoids wasting computation on weak candidates.
1129.po: On real-world graphs, the method found the largest possible groups of specified density more often than competing methods, with lower variance (more stable results). It runs fast enough for interactive recommendation systems, making it practical for platforms that need to discover product bundles or community-aware social recommendations in real time.

1130.bp: When someone looks for a question-answer pair on a platform like Stack Overflow or Quora, they want the question to match what they asked and the answer to actually solve the problem. The system has to understand both pieces together, not just rank them separately, because a great answer to a different question is useless.
1130.wh: Standard recommendation systems treat question-answer pairs as single units or focus only on the answer, missing that two different sources of confusion exist. First, user feedback ('they clicked this pair') is tangled—did they like the question, the answer, or both? Second, questions and answers have semantic correlations: related questions often have related answers, creating hidden structure that simple ranking ignores. This entanglement makes it hard to learn what the user actually values.
1130.ap: They build a graph neural network that creates two parallel graph views. The first view pulls questions and answers apart and models how users interact with each independently, disentangling collaborative information. The second view keeps questions and answers linked and models how they relate to each other—and how different Q&A pairs relate to each other—capturing semantic structure. These two views are then merged into a unified graph so the system can reason about both sources of information together.
1130.ww: By separating the two sources of confusion and then recombining them, the model can learn which part of user interest comes from collaborative patterns ('users like me tend to read this') and which part comes from semantic patterns ('questions with certain keywords attract certain answers'). This decomposition lets the model distinguish signal from noise in user feedback and navigate the complex relationships between Q&A elements.
1130.po: The recommendation quality improves because the system now correctly identifies which question and which answer matter most for each user. It also provides interpretability: you can see whether the recommendation was driven by collaborative or semantic reasoning, helping debug and improve the system further.

1131.bp: When people interact with online platforms through multiple modalities (reading articles, viewing images, watching videos), a personalized system that generates tailored content should understand their preference for text versus visual content. A user might like visual summaries but textual news, or vice versa. Treating all preferences as one blurs these differences.
1131.wh: Existing personalized generation methods either model user preferences as a single vector (losing modality specificity) or generate text and images independently (risking inconsistency—the image and text tell different stories). There's also a gap between how preferences are represented internally (as continuous numbers) and how generators need them (as discrete input tokens that fit into a language or image model). Bridging this gap is non-trivial.
1131.ap: They propose a two-stage framework. First, a graph neural network learns modal-specific preferences for each user: separate models for how much they like text-based content versus visual content, inferred from their interaction history. These continuous preference scores are then quantized into discrete tokens (like 'high-visual-preference-token'). Second, these discrete tokens are injected into text and image generators as conditioning information, guiding what content they produce. A consistency mechanism ensures the generated text and image tell a coherent story.
1131.ww: The reason this works is that preferences are modality-dependent (someone liking dense text doesn't mean they'll like busy images), and generators think in discrete tokens. By learning preferences separately and then embedding them as discrete tokens, the system respects both constraints. The consistency mechanism ensures the generators don't contradict each other because they see each other's outputs during generation.
1131.po: The system now generates personalized content that respects the user's modal preferences: if you prefer visual content, text-summaries are brief and images are detailed; if you prefer text, the reverse applies. Generated images and text align in meaning and tone, preventing jarring inconsistencies.

1132.bp: Databases, websites, and knowledge sources often describe the same real-world entity (a person, a company, a place) differently and use different identifiers. Matching entities across these sources is essential for integration and search, but it's context-dependent: the same name might refer to different people in different databases.
1132.wh: Supervised models trained on one dataset degrade when deployed on a new database because entity-matching rules vary by domain. A rule that works for matching people (check birthdate) doesn't work for products (no birthdate). With limited labeled examples of matches in a new domain, the model overfits or fails. Large language models are more flexible but inconsistent without massive labeled examples, and they can hallucinate false matches.
1132.ap: They convert a small set of labeled entity matches into explicit matching rules written in plain language (e.g., 'if the names are similar and locations match, link them'). They then cluster these rules into abstract meta-rules (e.g., 'similar-properties-and-location' is a meta-rule covering several specific rules). At deployment on a new entity pair, the system retrieves the most relevant meta-rules and uses them to guide a language model's reasoning. This grounding prevents the language model from drifting into hallucination.
1132.ww: Meta-rules work because they abstractly capture reusable logic. A rule 'match if names are identical' is too specific to one domain; a rule 'match if key properties overlap' is reusable across domains. By deriving meta-rules from limited labeled data and then retrieving the relevant ones for each entity pair, the system gets the flexibility of language models with the consistency of rule-based reasoning.
1132.po: The system can now match entities across new domains with minimal labeled data (scarce supervision) and remains robust: when the entity distribution shifts (new types of entities appear), it retrieves different meta-rules instead of collapsing. It's also interpretable—a user can see which rule guided each match decision.

1133.bp: Matching a product in a photo to a product in a database requires seeing both the image and the structured description, then deciding if they represent the same object. This is hard because an image and a database entry can both be right but look very different—the photo is at an angle, in different lighting, with background clutter.
1133.wh: Pretrained vision-language models compute similarity scores between an image and a structured description, but these scores are noisy for cross-modal data. Picking the best match for each entity independently can lead to inconsistent pairings: image A matches best to database B, but image B matches best to database A, which is logically impossible. Checking all large candidate sets with a powerful language model is too slow.
1133.ap: They build a multi-agent framework where agents iteratively propose and refine matches by combining multiple signals: similarity scores from a vision-language model, structural consistency checks (ensuring matches form a coherent global assignment), and selective queries to a multimodal language model for ambiguous cases. The framework uses a 'blackboard' (shared workspace) where agents leave their proposals and refinements, gradually converging toward a consistent matching.
1133.ww: The reason this works is that matching is both local and global: each image-database pair has local similarity, but the set of all pairings must be globally consistent (no two images match the same database entry). By iteratively enforcing local signals and global consistency, the system avoids the contradictions of independent ranking. Selectively invoking the expensive multimodal model for uncertain cases keeps computation practical.
1133.po: The system finds correct matches across image and structured-data collections without extensive labeling. It produces globally consistent matchings instead of contradictory local decisions, and it's fast enough for real-world data integration tasks because it uses the expensive language model only when needed, not for every candidate pair.

1134.bp: A temporal knowledge graph stores facts with time information: 'Alice was CEO in 2020' and 'Bob became CEO in 2021' are different facts. Answering questions about these graphs ('who was CEO in 2022?') requires reasoning about time and structure together. A language model alone can't answer without being shown the right facts.
1134.wh: Existing methods convert the time-annotated graph into plain text ('Alice was CEO of Corp in 2020') and treat it like a document-retrieval problem. But this loses structure: the system forgets that 'Alice,' 'CEO,' and 'Corp' are nodes in a graph with precise relationships. It retrieves the top-matching sentences by keyword similarity, which might miss relevant facts or include irrelevant noise, and it throws away information about which facts are linked.
1134.ap: They introduce a parser that reads the natural-language question and extracts a structured pattern (a subgraph shape: 'person-has-role-in-company') and temporal constraints ('between 2020 and 2022'). This pattern is used to directly retrieve a relevant subgraph from the knowledge graph, not top-n sentences. The retrieved subgraph is then compressed to remove less-relevant facts and fed to a language model for final reasoning.
1134.ww: Preserving structure throughout the pipeline preserves meaning. A pattern like 'person-has-role-in-company' is much more selective than keyword search and naturally handles temporal constraints (roles with specific time windows). By retrieving a structured subgraph instead of unordered text, the language model receives a coherent, focused context instead of a dense jumble of possibly-irrelevant facts.
1134.po: The system answers complex temporal questions more accurately than methods that lose structure by textualization. It also reduces noise in the context fed to the language model, so reasoning is clearer. The approach scales because structured subgraph retrieval is more efficient than ranking all document chunks.

1135.bp: In online advertising, an ad platform needs to decide how much to bid for an impression to maximize profit while avoiding overspending or underspending. This is a sequential decision problem: your bid today affects what you pay, what you learn, and what bids you make tomorrow. Balancing profit and risk is essential.
1135.wh: Rule-based bidding is predictable but rigid—it can't adapt to new campaign goals or market conditions. Reinforcement learning can adapt but struggles to plan far ahead (it myopically maximizes immediate reward). Recent generative approaches can think about longer sequences of decisions but often explore randomly or recklessly, risking large financial losses. They also lack a safety net: if exploration goes bad, there's no fallback.
1135.ap: They build a system using a Decision Transformer (a generative model that learns sequences of past actions and states and generates future actions). This generative core is paired with two complementary modules. A Q-value module (which estimates value of actions) guides exploration by regularizing the transformer's output toward valuable actions. An Inverse Dynamics Module (which predicts what actions would lead to observed outcomes) generates a behavioral fallback policy based on past successful patterns. If exploration looks risky, the system can fall back to known-good behavior.
1135.ww: The intuition is that generative models are flexible and can learn long-term dependencies, but they need guidance and safety. The Q-value module provides a compass (which directions are valuable). The inverse dynamics module provides a parachute (if the compass breaks, fall back to reproducing known-good behavior). Together, they let the system explore more efficiently without reckless financial risk.
1135.po: The system can bid in a way that balances exploration (learning about new campaign opportunities) and safety (not losing money on bad bids). It adapts better to changing market conditions than rule-based methods while maintaining lower financial risk than pure generative approaches. This makes automated bidding more reliable for advertising platforms.

1136.bp: An AI agent that searches the web to answer questions needs to think step-by-step: form a plan, search for information, read the results, refine the plan, repeat. These steps are serial—each step waits for the previous one to finish. This is slow, and users notice the delay. Can we use a faster model architecture to speed this up?
1136.wh: Diffusion language models generate all tokens in parallel (much faster than normal models that generate one token at a time), but existing diffusion models are weak at reasoning and tool use—they don't understand how to break down problems or call external tools correctly. Faster isn't useful if the agent gives wrong answers. The challenge is keeping the speed advantage while getting reasoning and tool abilities.
1136.ap: They train the diffusion model on two objectives: first, specialized supervised fine-tuning on agent behaviors (thinking step-by-step, calling the right tools with right arguments); second, a preference optimization method that rewards reasoning and tool-use correctness, penalizing hallucinated tool calls. They also redesign the agent loop to exploit parallelism: instead of waiting for each step serially, they generate multiple candidate next actions in parallel and filter them.
1136.ww: The reason this works is that specialized training and preference optimization can teach a weak base model strong reasoning skills. Parallel generation of candidates lets you try multiple search paths at once, then keep the best ones, instead of committing to one serial path. This multiplies the speed advantage of the diffusion model by reducing latency from serial waiting.
1136.po: Search agents now respond faster—the parallel nature of diffusion models removes waiting time between reasoning steps and tool calls. Accuracy is preserved because the training focuses on reasoning and tool-use correctness. This makes LLM-based search practical for user-facing applications where latency matters.

1137.bp: When a language model learns from data, it absorbs patterns from that data, including biases. If training data has gender bias (certain professions are male-skewed), a model trained on it will recommend careers in a gender-skewed way. For recommendation systems, this bias translates into unfair outcomes for users.
1137.wh: The core tension is that user preferences and sensitive attributes (gender, age) get tangled in the model's parameters. A naive approach—fine-tune the model to ignore gender—often hurts recommendation quality because the model can't distinguish between 'genuine preference' and 'preference correlated with gender.' Prompt engineering is unstable and doesn't change the underlying parameters where bias lives.
1137.ap: They use a mixture-of-experts architecture where different experts specialize in different tasks. Some experts learn to predict what a user will enjoy ('utility experts'). Other experts are trained adversarially to suppress gender information ('fairness experts'). A router network decides when to use each type of expert. A preference optimization method then fine-tunes the whole system to jointly maximize recommendation quality and fairness, not sacrificing one for the other.
1137.ww: The reason this works is separation of concerns: by splitting utility experts from fairness experts, the model can optimize the two objectives without conflicting parameters. The utility experts learn 'what people like,' while fairness experts learn 'what to filter out.' The router can then blend these signals intelligently per user. Preference optimization provides a unified training signal that avoids the quality-fairness tradeoff.
1137.po: The system generates recommendations that are both accurate (high-quality suggestions) and fair (balanced across gender and age groups) across multiple benchmarks and model types. Crucially, fairness improvements don't degrade recommendation quality, solving the traditional tradeoff.

1138.bp: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is predicting whether someone will click an ad or item they see. In recommender systems and advertising, this is fundamental to ranking what to show. Modeling user interest evolution (how interests shift over time and context) is key to accuracy.
1138.wh: Traditional machine learning methods treat each prediction independently and miss the sequential nature of user behavior: your next click depends on what you clicked before, and interests evolve as you see more items. Recent methods try to capture sequences but they're designed for static data snapshots, not the complex temporal and contextual patterns in recommendation logs. Combining multiple models (ensemble methods) is proven to help, but existing ensemble methods ignore the sequence aspect.
1138.ap: They design a diffusion-based ensemble framework that views multiple diverse CTR models as different perspectives on the same prediction problem. A diffusion model (which gradually refines initial guesses toward better guesses) learns to blend these perspectives intelligently, paying more attention to models that are confident on this particular prediction. They also build a behavior hypergraph capturing how users and items interact over time, and use it to inject structure-aware noise into the diffusion process, guiding exploration toward accurate predictions.
1138.ww: Diffusion models are good at exploration and refinement, so they naturally handle sequential data: each refinement step can use new temporal information. Hypergraph structure captures multi-way relationships (user-item-time-context interactions) better than standard graphs. By using the hypergraph to inform noise injection in diffusion, the model explores in directions that respect the behavioral structure of the data.
1138.po: CTR predictions are more accurate than single-model baselines and more efficient than naive ensembles, because the diffusion framework learns which models to trust and how to blend them for each context. The hypergraph formulation also scales to large real-world datasets, making this practical for large-scale recommendation systems.

1139.bp: Companies collect personal data (name, email, location, browsing history) and must explain in a privacy policy why they collect it and how it's used. Laws like GDPR require that data collection follow a principle of minimization: collect only data that's necessary for the stated purpose. If you're building a weather app, collecting the user's political leanings isn't necessary and violates the minimization principle.
1139.wh: Privacy policies are long, unstructured, and semantic ally vague. What counts as 'necessary' is context-dependent: a financial app might need income information, but a social app doesn't. Manually reviewing thousands of policies is expensive, and automated detection requires understanding fine-grained data practices—not just that 'location is collected' but 'location is collected for ad targeting, which isn't strictly necessary for the app's core function.'
1139.ap: They build a framework combining human expertise and language models. First, they identify two types of violations: inherent ones (collecting sensitive data like health records for frivolous purposes) and contextual ones (collecting more data than necessary for a stated purpose). They extract compliance patterns from large policy datasets and integrate expert knowledge about legitimate uses. Then, for each policy, they use humans and language models to jointly evaluate whether data collection adheres to the minimization principle.
1139.ww: The reason this works is that minimization is a nuanced judgment requiring both data understanding (what's collected) and domain knowledge (what's necessary for which purposes). Language models are good at extracting data practices from text, but they hallucinate about necessity. Humans are good at judgment but expensive. By automating extraction and using human judgment selectively on ambiguous cases (the collaboration), the framework scales without sacrificing accuracy.
1139.po: The system can automatically flag data practices that violate the minimization principle in privacy policies, helping companies comply with regulation and helping regulators audit compliance at scale. It identifies both obvious violations (collecting health data for a game app) and subtle ones (collecting more precise location than necessary).
